strengths: The framework addresses a relevant problem: constructing reusable discrete EEG representations. Combining localized spectral encoding with raw-signal features is a sensible design, and retaining discrete tokens during downstream inference distinguishes it from LaBraM’s training-only tokenizer.

Evaluation covers four clinical EEG datasets, seven baselines, and five random seeds. TFM-Token achieves the best reported mean performance across the evaluated metrics, with particularly encouraging results on IIIC and TUAB.

The paper includes useful ablations of input domains, masking, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, and masked-token pretraining. Replacing LaBraM’s tokenizer also improves its reported results, providing evidence that the tokenizer contributes beyond the proposed classifier.

The appendix provides architecture settings, training hyperparameters, preprocessing details, and dataset splits. Retrieval experiments and waveform visualizations offer useful exploratory evidence about the learned tokens.
weaknesses: The frequency-preservation analysis in Section 5.3 does not establish its central claim. Fourier analysis of discrete token IDs depends on arbitrary codebook numbering: permuting IDs can change spectral entropy without changing the representation. If embeddings are analyzed instead, their treatment is unspecified. Moreover, greater temporal variation in token representations does not demonstrate preservation of physiological high-frequency content. Frequency-resolved reconstruction or controlled signal probes are needed.

The claimed scalability and generalization are not demonstrated. Appendix B.1 specifies separate tokenizer training, encoder pretraining, and fine-tuning within each dataset. There is no frozen-tokenizer transfer across datasets, channel-count sweep, single-channel downstream evaluation, or missing-channel experiment. Channel-independent tokenization is architecturally plausible, but the experiments do not validate the broader adaptability and robustness claims.

The evaluation cannot isolate the benefit of discretization. There is no matched continuous version of the same dual-path architecture, nor sufficient controls separating frequency patching, gated aggregation, quantization, and model size. The raw-only and STFT-only variants address input modalities but do not establish that discrete tokens cause the improvements or parameter savings.

The state-of-the-art claims exceed the comparison scope. BIOT and LaBraM are retrained within individual datasets, and LaBraM uses a changed channel configuration. This is a useful controlled setting, but it does not establish superiority over their pretrained foundation-model configurations. The proposed method receives extensive hyperparameter optimization, while equivalent baseline search budgets are not documented.

Several headline gains are uncertain relative to the reported variability. On TUEV, balanced accuracy improves from 0.4682 ± 0.0856 to 0.4943 ± 0.0516; the joint model also only slightly exceeds its raw-only variant. CHB-MIT balanced accuracy improves from 0.6717 to 0.6750. Paired comparisons or confidence intervals are needed before describing these improvements as significant or consistently compelling.

Novelty is primarily an integration of established VQ-VAE, time-frequency encoding, masking, and transformer components. The claimed distinction that this method quantizes patches along time whereas conventional visual VQ methods quantize along embedding dimensions is misleading: standard visual VQ also assigns complete local embedding vectors to codebook entries. The methodological contribution needs more precise positioning.

The token-quality evidence is overinterpreted. Low codebook utilization can indicate collapse rather than desirable compactness, and class-exclusive token counts are sensitive to class sizes and rare occurrences. The selected waveform examples do not establish clinical meaning or invariance. Frequency-controlled analyses, token-frequency distributions, and systematic perturbation tests would provide stronger support.

Some implementation details remain unresolved despite the extensive appendix: the exact linear-attention variant, loss coefficients, EMA settings, and complete masking configuration are unspecified. Also, the raw branch receives the unmasked signal while reconstructing its masked spectrogram, leaving a direct route to the target and weakening the interpretation of this objective as learning missing time-frequency structure.

strengths: The framework addresses a relevant problem: learning discrete EEG representations using complementary waveform and spectral information. Separating a channel-wise tokenizer from a downstream multichannel encoder is a useful design.

Evaluation covers four clinical EEG datasets, uses several established baselines, and reports means and standard deviations over five seeds. TFM-Token achieves the best reported mean performance across the principal classification metrics, with particularly encouraging results on IIIC and TUAB.

The paper includes useful component ablations, token retrieval experiments, and a tokenizer replacement experiment within LaBraM. Architecture and training tables provide substantial implementation detail.
weaknesses: The frequency-learning analysis in Section 5.3 does not establish its central claim. Applying a Fourier transform to discrete token IDs produces results that depend on arbitrary codebook numbering: relabeling otherwise identical tokens can change the spectrum. If embeddings are used instead, their treatment is unspecified. Moreover, higher spectral entropy of a token sequence does not demonstrate preservation of physiological high-frequency information. Frequency-controlled probes or band-specific reconstruction measurements are needed.

The claimed generalization across tasks and channel configurations is not demonstrated. Appendix B.1 explicitly trains a separate tokenizer and encoder within each dataset. There is no transfer of a frozen tokenizer between datasets, evaluation under changing channel configurations, or direct single-channel downstream evaluation. Replacing LaBraM's tokenizer within the same dataset establishes compatibility, not broad transferability.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of discretization. There is no matched continuous version of the same dual-path architecture with comparable training and capacity. Consequently, improvements could arise from spectral processing, architecture, or optimization rather than discrete tokens. The raw-only and STFT-only variants do not resolve this confound.

The state-of-the-art claim exceeds the comparison setting. BIOT and LaBraM are retrained within individual datasets, excluding the large-scale pretraining central to their foundation-model use. This is a reasonable controlled setting, but it supports superiority over these restricted reproductions rather than over the full methods. The proposed model receives extensive hyperparameter optimization, while comparable baseline tuning budgets are not documented.

Several highlighted gains are small relative to the reported variability. On TUEV, balanced accuracy is 0.4943 ± 0.0516 versus 0.4682 ± 0.0856 for LaBraM and 0.4898 ± 0.0105 for the raw-only variant. On CHB-MIT, balanced accuracy is 0.6750 ± 0.0392 versus 0.6717 ± 0.0271 for ST-Transformer. Paired comparisons or confidence intervals are needed to support strong superiority claims; five-seed standard deviations alone do not establish them.

The token-quality evidence is overinterpreted. Utilization below 10% could indicate codebook underuse rather than beneficial compression. Class-exclusive token counts depend on sample size, class balance, and token rarity, and do not establish clinically meaningful motifs. Figure 5 provides illustrative examples without systematic stability measurements or expert validation. These analyses do not substantiate the broad robustness and interpretability claims.

The methodological novelty is primarily a combination of established VQ learning, spectral processing, masking, and transformer components. The claimed distinction from conventional image VQ is misleading: standard VQ tokenizers also assign codebook vectors to individual patch or spatial embeddings. Additionally, the unmasked raw-signal branch contains the information needed to reconstruct masked spectral regions, weakening the interpretation of masking as forcing contextual frequency inference. This shortcut should be explicitly tested.

strengths: The framework addresses a relevant EEG representation problem with a coherent combination of raw-signal features, localized spectral modeling, discrete quantization, and masked token prediction.

Evaluation covers four clinical EEG datasets, seven baselines, and five random seeds. Reported mean performance consistently improves over the reproduced baselines, with particularly encouraging results on TUAB and IIIC.

The paper includes useful component ablations, token retrieval experiments, qualitative motif visualizations, and a tokenizer replacement experiment in LaBraM. The appendix provides substantial architectural and training details.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discretization is not isolated. There is no matched continuous-representation version using the same dual-domain encoder, training objectives, and capacity. Consequently, improvements could come from spectral processing or architectural choices rather than discrete tokens. Most components are established techniques, and the claim that conventional visual VQ quantizes embedding dimensions rather than individual patch vectors mischaracterizes standard VQ-VAE tokenization.

The frequency-learning analysis in Section 5.3 does not substantiate the claimed preservation of EEG frequency content. A Fourier transform of numerical token IDs depends on arbitrary codebook numbering; if embeddings are used instead, the representation and aggregation procedure need specification. In either case, greater spectral entropy of a token sequence does not establish better preservation of physiological frequency bands, and noise can also increase entropy.

Generalization and scalability claims substantially exceed the experiments. Each tokenizer and encoder is trained separately within each dataset. There is no transfer of a fixed tokenizer across datasets, devices, or channel configurations, nor a downstream single-channel or missing-channel evaluation. Replacing LaBraM's tokenizer within the same dataset demonstrates compatibility, not cross-setting generalization.

The comparisons support performance under a restricted training regime rather than broad state-of-the-art claims. BIOT and LaBraM are retrained within individual datasets rather than evaluated with their large-scale pretraining. This is a useful controlled setting, but pretrained-checkpoint comparisons and comparable baseline tuning budgets are needed to establish competitiveness with foundation models.

Several highlighted gains have substantial uncertainty. On TUEV, balanced accuracy is 0.4943 ± 0.0516 versus 0.4682 ± 0.0856 for LaBraM; on CHB-MIT, AUC-PR is 0.3379 ± 0.0515 versus 0.3127 ± 0.0890 for BIOT. Paired results or confidence intervals are needed to support strong improvement claims. Statements of statistical significance in the ablations are not accompanied by statistical tests.

Token quality and interpretability conclusions are overstated. Utilization below 10% could indicate codebook underuse rather than desirable compression, while class-exclusive token counts depend on token rarity and sample size. Six selected waveform examples do not establish clinical interpretability or robustness. Frequency-specific reconstruction tests, token stability measurements, and expert assessment would provide stronger evidence.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting remain incomplete: the precise linear-attention implementation, loss weights, EMA settings, and several masking details are unspecified. Parameter counts alone do not demonstrate computational scalability, and the accounting should clearly separate tokenizer, decoder, classifier, and total inference parameters, with runtime and memory measurements.

strengths: The reusable, channel-independent EEG tokenizer addresses a relevant problem: transferring learned representations across channel configurations and downstream architectures.
The compact 1.9M-parameter pipeline achieves promising results, notably improving multi-dataset TUEV Cohen’s kappa from 0.5273 to 0.6189 while outperforming substantially larger evaluated models.

Evaluation covers four EEG benchmarks and an ear-EEG transfer task, reports five-seed variability, and includes useful ablations on masking, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, and downstream depth.
Subject-wise splits for IIIC, CHB-MIT, and ear-EEG, together with detailed architecture and optimization tables, are positive experimental practices.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discrete tokenization is not isolated. There is no matched continuous-feature baseline using the same dual-path encoder, downstream architecture, and training budget, nor a comparison feeding LaBraM’s discrete codes directly into the same downstream model. Consequently, improvements could arise from the encoder or training procedure rather than the proposed discrete interface. The architectural contribution otherwise combines established VQ, spectral processing, gating, and masked modeling components.

Several headline gains depend on unexpectedly weak pretrained baselines. On IIIC, vanilla BIOT achieves 0.4932 kappa, whereas reproduced single- and multi-dataset pretrained BIOT obtain 0.3418 and 0.3362. The claimed 36% improvement over multi-dataset LaBraM therefore contrasts with only a small advantage over vanilla BIOT. This degradation needs investigation and comparable baseline tuning before strong superiority claims are justified.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 does not establish the claimed mechanism. Fourier analysis of numerical token IDs depends on arbitrary codebook labeling; if embeddings were analyzed instead, their treatment is unspecified. Moreover, higher spectral entropy can reflect noise or rapid token switching rather than preservation of meaningful EEG frequency content.

Token interpretability evidence is limited. Class-exclusive token counts depend on sample size, class frequency, and token rarity, while reduced codebook utilization does not by itself demonstrate better compression or less redundancy. Selected waveform examples and within-class retrieval do not establish physiological motif validity or robustness to amplitude changes and temporal warping.

Generalization claims exceed the evaluation. Ear-EEG testing uses only two held-out subjects and supervised target-domain fine-tuning, without sleep-specific baselines or subject-level uncertainty. The LaBraM integration replaces its tokenizer during masked EEG modeling, so it does not directly demonstrate the advertised use of discrete tokens as downstream inputs across architectures.

Claims of consistent improvements overlook material exceptions. Multi-dataset CHB-MIT balanced accuracy is 0.6471 versus BIOT’s 0.7068; Table 9 also shows several decreases after tokenizer integration. Its stated improvement rate of 93% is inconsistent with the 31 improvements among 36 reported metric comparisons.

Important training details remain unclear: masking ratios, how frequency masking interacts with the raw-signal branch, reconstruction over masked versus all positions, loss coefficients, and codebook EMA settings. Without specifying how the raw branch is masked, information leakage between reconstruction targets and encoder inputs cannot be assessed. Statistical significance claims also lack a stated testing procedure.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: reusable EEG representations that accommodate different channel configurations. The single-channel tokenizer and compact downstream transformer form a plausible, practical architecture.

Provides substantial empirical coverage across four EEG benchmarks, an ear-EEG transfer task, and five random seeds. The multi-dataset TUEV improvement in Cohen’s kappa from 0.5273 to 0.6189 is encouraging.
Includes useful ablations on input domains, masking, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, and downstream depth, alongside architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discrete tokenization is not established. There is no matched comparison using the same dual-path encoder and downstream architecture with continuous embeddings instead of quantization, nor a direct comparison using LaBraM token embeddings as downstream inputs. Consequently, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed discrete motif vocabulary rather than feature extraction or training choices.

Some headline comparisons exaggerate the evidence. The reported 36% IIIC improvement compares against a multi-dataset LaBraM kappa of 0.3658, although vanilla BIOT already achieves 0.4932 versus the proposed method’s 0.4979. The substantial deterioration of pretrained BIOT relative to vanilla BIOT remains unexplained. Claims of consistently outperforming all baselines also conflict with CHB-MIT balanced accuracy: 0.6471 versus BIOT’s 0.7068.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 is not technically convincing. Fourier analysis of discrete token IDs depends on arbitrary codebook numbering; renumbering tokens can change spectral entropy without changing their information. If embeddings are analyzed instead, the representation and aggregation procedure require specification. Higher token-sequence entropy alone does not establish preservation of physiologically meaningful frequency information.

Evidence for meaningful, robust motifs is limited. Class-token uniqueness depends on sample frequency and class coverage, while low codebook utilization can indicate collapse rather than desirable compression. Selected waveform examples and label-based retrieval do not establish invariance to noise, amplitude scaling, or temporal warping. Controlled perturbation experiments and quantitative physiological validation are missing.

The foundation-model integration claim is narrower than presented. For LaBraM, the method replaces the tokenizer used as a pretraining target, rather than demonstrating the advertised reusable discrete-input interface. Table 9 also includes substantial balanced-accuracy regressions for BIOT, so integration benefits are metric-dependent.

Cross-device generalization rests on one ear-EEG dataset with only two held-out test subjects and supervised fine-tuning. This is useful preliminary evidence, but insufficient for broad device-agnostic claims. Variation across random seeds does not measure uncertainty across subjects, and the reported significance tests lack sufficient methodological detail.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including masking rates, reconstruction-loss weights, and how frequency masking interacts with the raw-signal branch, which could expose information removed from the spectral input. Together with the missing controls and weaknesses in the token analyses, these gaps leave the main contribution insufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reusable EEG tokenization that accommodates different channel configurations. The single-channel tokenizer and separate cross-channel model form a coherent, practical architecture.
The evaluation covers four clinical EEG benchmarks, two backbone integrations, and an ear-EEG transfer task, with results reported over five random seeds.

Several improvements are substantial. Under multi-dataset pretraining, TUEV Cohen’s kappa increases from 0.5273 for BIOT to 0.6189, using a smaller reported model. TUAB results also consistently favor the proposed method.
The appendix provides useful architectural details and ablations on input domains, masking, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, and downstream depth.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central contribution of discrete tokenization. A matched continuous version of the same dual-path encoder, trained with comparable objectives and compute, is missing. Consequently, improvements could arise from the spectral architecture or training recipe rather than the learned vocabulary. The frequency transformer and gated aggregation also lack individual ablations.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 is not a valid demonstration of richer EEG frequency representations as described. Fourier analysis of discrete token IDs depends on arbitrary codebook numbering: relabeling identical tokens can change the measured spectrum without changing their meaning. If embeddings were analyzed instead, the representation and aggregation procedure need specification. Higher token-sequence spectral entropy alone does not establish preservation of physiological frequency content.

Some headline comparisons overstate the evidence. The reported 36% IIIC kappa gain compares against a multi-dataset LaBraM result of 0.3658, while vanilla BIOT already achieves 0.4932 versus the proposed 0.4979. The substantial deterioration of pretrained BIOT relative to vanilla BIOT requires investigation. Moreover, multi-dataset CHB-MIT balanced accuracy is lower than BIOT’s, contradicting blanket claims of consistently outperforming all baselines.

The claimed reusable-input interface is not demonstrated consistently across backbones. Section 4.3 describes replacing LaBraM’s tokenizer during masked EEG modeling, which changes its pretraining targets; it does not establish that LaBraM consumes the proposed discrete tokens during downstream inference. This distinction matters because the paper explicitly motivates its contribution by criticizing target-only tokenization.

The interpretation of token quality is too strong. Low codebook utilization can indicate collapse rather than useful compression, and class-exclusive tokens can reflect rare occurrences or dataset-specific artifacts. The selected waveform examples lack expert validation or systematic perturbation tests establishing physiological meaning and robustness.

Cross-device evidence is promising but limited to one ear-EEG dataset with two held-out test subjects and supervised target-task fine-tuning. This supports transfer feasibility, but broad device generalization needs additional subject splits, device settings, and task-specific sleep-staging baselines.

Important methodological details remain unclear, including masking rates, reconstruction-loss restriction to masked regions, treatment of the raw-signal branch during frequency masking, and codebook-loss coefficients. Significance claims do not identify the statistical test, and several modest ablation improvements are small relative to reported variability. Together with the missing controlled baselines, these issues leave the central claims insufficiently established for acceptance.
